                        IntroductionRainfall from the West African monsoon (WAM) is the cornerstone of food security and the economy for hundreds of millions of people1,2. The WAM affords more than 80% of the total annual rainfall necessary for food production and livelihoods. Disentangling plausible pathways of WAM rainfall projections is therefore crucial for supporting climate services that inform sustainable adaptation strategies. The region, however, remains one of the greatest challenges for global climate modelling. Climate models’ development has advanced dramatically, but global projections of the WAM are still fraught with persistent divergences within the models3,4.The advent of the sixth phase of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP65) has brought improvements in resolution and process complexity. Nevertheless, precipitation projections for West Africa throughout the 21st century still show considerable spread, ranging from significant increases in wetness to severe drying6,7. The lack of consensus among models is largely attributed to systematic biases in the simulation of large-scale atmospheric dynamics, particularly the pressure gradient between the Sahara and the South Atlantic Ocean, as well as the representation of low-level moisture fluxes8,9. The canonical practice of using the ensemble mean (EnsMean) is increasingly criticized because it treats models with radically different physical performances equally10,11,12.The question of what plausible trajectories WAM precipitation will follow remains timely. Assessment approaches based on physical processes and mechanisms underpinning the monsoon system have been suggested to replace the former simple quantification of performance against observations13. This is because performance-based evaluation does not guarantee that the model plausibly reproduces the observed climatology, i.e., that the processes underlying simulated climatology are those behind observed ones. Furthermore, it is difficult to derive performance metrics to constrain future projections, since historical accuracy does not guarantee future reliability. This highlights the need for emergent constraints, which link observable variations in the contemporary climate to the long-term sensitivity of the climate system11,14. The process-oriented evaluation approaches consist of giving more credence to models that are able to simulate plausible processes associated with projected patterns. A plausible process can be identified in observations/reanalyses or is likely to occur, i.e. physically explainable, under global warming. This approach is also limited because it cannot go beyond the most state-of-the-art knowledge we have of the functioning of the climate system. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in climate science offers an opportunity to overcome this limitation. Indeed, deep learning, and more specifically artificial neural networks (ANNs), offer an unprecedented ability to extract complex spatial features, linear and non-linear relationships within large climate datasets15,16,17. Unlike traditional linear regression methods, ANNs excel at mapping interconnected and multi-dimensional teleconnection patterns, such as multi-pole sea surface temperature (SST) or pressure anomalies15, to local/regional variables, thereby reducing reliance on performance metrics derived solely from raw model outputs and the systematic biases associated with them.In this study, we propose a physical fidelity weighting approach combining deep learning with climate projections and reanalyses. This approach utilizes the Sahelian monsoon ocean-pressure index (SMOPI; see the “Methods” section), as a key spatiotemporal tracer of WAM rainfall18. We train ANNs to learn the dynamic relationship between the spatiotemporal structures of sea level pressure boxes of the SMOPI and monsoon precipitation. Using the Japanese 55-year reanalysis (JRA-5519) as a ground truth reference to force these pre-trained models, we quantify the degree of physical realism of the 11 CMIP6 models (see Supplementary Table 1). Raw projections are thus converted into an ANN-forced weighted ensemble where each model contributes proportionally to its demonstrated ability to reproduce observed teleconnections. Our results show that this approach reduces the inter-model spread by up to 30%. It also corrects the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of precipitation, making the distribution closer to historical observations, thereby increasing the plausibility of projections, as demonstrated by the pseudo-observation method (see the subsection “The pseudo-observation approach” in the “Methods” section). Furthermore, models with physically consistent teleconnections project clearer emerging shifts in precipitation distributions because they more accurately translate large-scale oceanic and dynamical signals into regional rainfall responses. By validating our approach on independent members (inter-member transfer learning from Member 1 to Member 2; see the subsection “ANNs: model architecture and training protocol” in the “Methods” section), we demonstrate the temporal stability of this learned physical relationship. This work offers a new way to constrain regional climate projections, thus providing a more robust scientific basis for resilience policies in West Africa.ResultsANNs capture how WAM precipitation responds to SMOPI SLP boxesThe first step involves informing the ANNs of the physics underlying the WAM precipitation. This is a complex task because the forcing factors of the WAM system operate across multiple scales, from local processes to global phenomena20. Furthermore, these factors act on timescales ranging from synoptic events to multi-decadal cycles. The WAM system is more than just a reversal of the ocean-continent thermal and pressure contrasts, often simplified as a large-scale sea breeze, that transports oceanic moisture inland. It is also an integral part of the energetic reorganization of tropical overturning circulations, including the Walker and Hadley cells, and the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ)21. Consequently, the WAM is influenced by large-scale teleconnections originating from the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans. The choice of the predictor is therefore critical, as it must account for the WAM’s specific complexity while remaining as simple as possible so that the ANN model can learn both linear and non-linear drivers of the WAM precipitation without overfitting. The Sahel monsoon ocean-pressure index (SMOPI) appears to be the most appropriate in this context (see the subsection “SMOPI” in the “Methods” section). The effectiveness of monsoon monitoring relies on the indicator’s ability to integrate multidimensional processes. It is demonstrated that the SMOPI captures not only regional drivers in the Sahel but also global teleconnections, while remaining effective across sub-seasonal to multi-decadal timescales18. These include, among others, the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO22), the Atlantic Meridional Mode (AMM23), and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD24), to name a few. In addition, the SMOPI explains the dominant mode of interannual variability in Sahelian rainfall (PC1, up to 74.4% of total variance), exhibiting strong interannual correlations (up to r = 0.75 in reanalyses)18. A remarkable result emerges when the analysis is extended to the entire West African region: the identified sea-level pressure (SLP) boxes remain almost identical and consistent (Supplementary Fig. 1), which is not surprising, as the Sahel monsoonal rainfall is just a regional expression of a larger WAM system20,25. This indicates that SMOPI can also be extended at the scale of the whole WAM system. Therefore, we used the five SMOPI’s SLP boxes (Supplementary Fig. 1) as input predictors, with the June–July–August–September (JJAS) monsoon precipitation being the predictand. The physically-derived SLP boxes are provided to the ANN without imposing the SMOPI formulation18, thereby allowing the ANN to learn its own dynamical relationship between circulation and rainfall. An attribution analysis based on Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) revealed that within the SMOPI signal, regional drivers heavily dominate the direct circulation-rainfall coupling over remote basins (Mouassom et al., under review). Specifically, the local Sahel landmass (Box 1, 54.63%) and the northern tropical Atlantic (Box 5, 32.55%) explain the vast majority of the model’s physical importance. Indeed, Box 1 (Supplementary Fig. 1) directly samples the core of the monsoon engine, where surface pressure variability reflects the intensity of the Saharan heat low (SHL) and low-level moisture convergence26. This strong local coupling is consistent with the established role of the SHL as a key driver regulating the WAM onset and intensity27. Meanwhile, Box 5 regulates the thermodynamic boundary governing low-level oceanic moisture advection, anchoring the critical SST gradients that feed moisture into the Sahelian interior28. Conversely, the footprints of remote oceanic basins from the southern Atlantic (Box 2, 8.46%), the tropical Pacific/ENSO (Box 4, 3.09%), and the southern Indian Ocean (Box 3, 1.27%) exhibit much smaller direct surface pressure weights. This lower direct weight aligns with the understanding that their physical influence on the monsoon acts mainly through indirect upper-tropospheric wave propagation and teleconnected regional subsidence rather than localized surface pressure gradients, as widely documented for ENSO29 and Mediterranean/Indian Ocean remote forcings30. The idea is to use the trained ANN model to project plausible future changes in the WAM precipitation under SSP5-8.5 warming scenarios. Given the importance of spatial variability within these boxes in shaping the SMOPI strength18, we used a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture (see the subsection “ANNs: model architecture and training protocol” in the “Methods” section), an AI model from the ANNs’ family, which is well-suited for extracting spatial features from gridded data31. CNNs effectively represent sub-regional atmospheric structures and capture complex non-linear interactions missed by traditional physics-based models.As previously mentioned, one of the prerequisites for a climate model to project a plausible future is its ability to realistically represent the historical climate and its underlying physical mechanisms. However, it is well-documented that many CMIP6 models struggle to accurately reproduce the WAM rainfall32. Some models exhibit structural biases linked to their internal physics, while others show biases stemming from the chaotic nature of their internal variability. Furthermore, the multi-model EnsMean is often not physically representative of any single member due to the cancellation of individual structural errors. To overcome these issues, we used a model’s cross-domain generalization approach17,33 to build a physics-weighted ANNs-based ensemble: we train each ANN individually on the raw outputs of CMIP6 models. Subsequently, each trained ANN is forced with the same reference data, in this study, the SLP boxes from JRA-55, used as predictors. Finally, the WAM precipitation (JJAS) predicted by each ANN is compared against observed rainfall data to evaluate the fidelity of the model’s physics relative to JRA-55 (Fig. 1, Supplementary Fig. 2). JRA-55 is used as the reference because it represents the intraseasonal and interannual precipitation variability more accurately than ERA5. It also better captures the teleconnections related to the SMOPI18. All ANNs-based predictions show a stronger correlation with observations (Fisher z-transform and back-transformed correlation, see the subsection “ANNs: model architecture and training protocol” in the “Methods” section) than with the raw data from CMIP6 (Fig. 1a). The correlation value of each model is used to estimate its weight wi in the ANNs-based EnsMean (see the subsection “ANNs’ ensemble-mean construction approach” in the “Methods” section). Here, the weight of each model in the constructed ANNs-based EnsMean is proportional to the strength of its correlation. The raw CMIP6 EnsMean, meanwhile, is computed using the traditional ‘model democracy’ method, which assumes that all models are equally realistic and therefore have the same weight. The ANNs-based EnsMean physics-weighted (Fig. 1c) shows much better statistical metrics (r > 0.81 and RMSE = 0.54) than the raw CMIP6 EnsMean (Fig. 1b; r < 0.65 and RMSE > 0.70). Moreover, all ANNs-based predictions improve the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of monsoon precipitation. While raw CMIP6 models tend to saturate at higher precipitation values than observed (Fig. 1d), they also exhibit an earlier onset of the cumulative distribution, revealing an overrepresentation of low-intensity rainfall. The cumulative distributions of JJAS precipitation show a substantial improvement across all intensity ranges for all ANNs (Fig. 1e). The early onset and delayed saturation observed in raw CMIP6 outputs are largely corrected, resulting in distributions that closely match CRU and GPCC observations. The raw CMIP6 EnsMean exhibits a substantial discrepancy from observations, with a Wasserstein distance (WD) value of WD = 0.83 (see the subsection “ANNs: model architecture and training protocol” in the “Methods” section), whereas the ANN physics-weighted EnsMean drastically reduces this distance (WD = 0.08).Fig. 1: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) input with the SMOPI sea-level pressure (SLP) boxes improve WAM precipitation.Full size imagea Comparison of Fisher z-transform and back-transformed correlation coefficients for June–September (JJAS) precipitation between raw CMIP6 models (gold) and ANN-based estimates (grey). All ANNs were pre-trained on individual CMIP6 historical (1958–2014) simulations and subsequently forced using SLP fields from the JRA-55 reanalysis. Correlations are calculated against JRA-55 precipitation, showing consistent improvement across all 11 CMIP6 models when using the ANN. Performance of the multi-model ensemble mean (EnsMean) for raw CMIP6 (b) and the EnsMean physics-weighted ANNs (c) against two observational datasets: CRU (orange) and GPCC (blue). Scatter plots show the regression of modelled/predicted JJAS precipitation against observations. The ANN-EnsMean (c) exhibits a higher Pearson correlation (r) and coefficient of determination (R2), and a lower root-mean-square error (RMSE) compared to raw CMIP6 outputs. Equations for the linear regression lines are provided for both datasets. Cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of JJAS precipitation (mm/day) for raw CMIP6 models (d) and their corresponding ANN-forced versions (e). In both panels, individual models are represented by thin coloured lines, while the ensemble mean is shown as a thick black line. Observational benchmarks (CRU and GPCC) are indicated by dotted blue and red lines, respectively. The Wasserstein distance (WD), representing the statistical distance between each model’s distribution and the CRU observation, is indicated in parentheses. The WD ANN values are in bold. The ANN approach significantly reduces the WD (e.g., from 0.83 to 0.08 for the EnsMean), demonstrating a superior ability to capture the frequency and intensity of WAM precipitation.Thus, the precipitation predicted by ANNs when forced by JRA-55 reanalysis data is more realistic than the raw simulations from CMIP6 models. One can easily attribute this to the fact that the SLP boxes derived from JRA-55 are dynamically consistent and observationally constrained because the reanalyses are obtained by assimilation that includes observations. However, even when using the same configuration and hyperparameters, different ANNs exhibit varying levels of skill compared to observations. It is therefore worth asking why some ANNs are better than others. Are the ANN predictions credible? In other words, are they realistic in relation to the realism of the teleconnections that they have learned from the corresponding driving raw CMIP6?More realistic teleconnections condition ANNs’ fidelityAnswering the questions above is a necessary step toward evaluating the plausibility of ANN projections. Since all the ANNs used for training are identical, it is easy to hypothesize that the differences do not stem from their configuration. Instead, we focus our attention on the raw CMIP6 models used to train the ANNs. To this, we investigated the accuracy of the teleconnections learned by each ANN. At first sight, two distinct model groups are highlighted: (1) the first group consists of models where the high performance of the derived ANNs is associated with a more realistic representation of teleconnections compared to reanalyses (see Supplementary Fig. 3). This includes models such as EC-Earth3, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, and MPI-ESM1-2-LR. (2) The second group includes models in which, although the derived ANNs predict precipitation more accurately than the corresponding raw models, they exhibit teleconnection patterns that differ from those in reanalyses and are therefore unrealistic. This group includes ACCESS-CM2, ACCESS-ESM1-5, CanESM5, CESM2, CESM2-WACCM, CNRM-ESM2-1, and MRI-ESM2-0 (see Supplementary Fig. 3). We statistically quantified the performance of each group across the five SMOPI SLP boxes using pattern correlation (Fig. 2a; spatial resemblance) and the Taylor Skill Score (TSS, Fig. 2b; spatial resemblance and amplitude bias). The results show that for all models in the first group, at least 3 out of 5 SLP boxes have strong, positive, and significant (p < 0.05) correlations and TSS values compared to reanalyses (hereafter referred to as “best models (BEST)”). In contrast, models in the second group exhibit low or sometimes negative correlations and TSS values in most SLP boxes (hereafter referred to as “remaining models (RESM)”). Building on this classification, we evaluated the multi-decadal variability of the SMOPI intensity itself (ISMOPI) as seen from the two model groups. By comparing the ensemble mean of the BESTs (BEST-EnsMean) and that of the RESMs (RESM-EnsMean) against reanalyses, we find that the BEST-EnsMean provides a more realistic representation of the SMOPI (r > 0.84, p < 0.01) than the RESM-EnsMean (r < 0.76, p < 0.01; Fig. 2c). Consistently, the BEST-EnsMean displays a more realistic spatial structure of teleconnections between the SMOPI SLP boxes and WAM precipitation than that of the RESM-EnsMean (Supplementary Fig. 4). Furthermore, some individual model performance reflects this trend: for instance, MIROC6, from the BESTs group, shows a SMOPI variability highly similar to the references (r > 0.71, p < 0.01), whereas ACCESS-CM2, from the RESMs group, fails to capture this variability (r < −0.14; Fig. 2d). However, it is worth noting that some RESMs show better SMOPI correlations than some BESTs (Supplementary Fig. 5) despite their inconsistent spatial structure of teleconnections (Supplementary Fig. 3), meaning that high correlations of SMOPI do not always indicate the underlying physics are correct. Such a model achieves good results, but for the wrong reasons, likely in association with error compensation in its internal physics or a random statistical association. We therefore argue that high SMOPI correlations alone are not enough to prove a model is reliable. Thus, subject to further evaluation of their plausibility, ANNs trained on BESTs are more dependable for future projections because their results are based on a more realistic representation of the physical drivers of the WAM system.Fig. 2: Realistic representation of SLP teleconnections determines the fidelity of ANN precipitation estimates.Full size imageEvaluation of the representation of the five sea-level pressure (SLP) predictor boxes (SLP1-SLP5) across the 11 CMIP6 models. Performance is quantified using a spatial pattern correlation and b Taylor Skill Score (TSS) against JRA-55 and ERA5 reanalyses. Higher values (dark red in a, dark green in b) signify better alignment with reanalysis benchmarks. c Time series of the SMOPI index (ISMOPI) from 1958 to 2014 for the high-performing ensemble mean (BEST-EnsMean, blue) and the remaining model ensemble mean (RESM-EnsMean, gold), compared against JRA-55 (black) and ERA5 (green) reanalyses. The BEST-EnsMean is composed of models (blue colour in panels a and b) demonstrating high pattern correlation and TSS in at least three of the five SLP predictor boxes, while RESM-EnsMean includes the remaining models (gold colour in panels a and b). Correlation coefficients (r) against reanalyses are indicated; asterisks (*) denote statistical significance at the p < 0.01 confidence level. d Comparison of ISMOPI for a representative high-fidelity model from the BEST-EnsMean group (MIROC6, blue) and a low-fidelity model from the RESM-EnsMean group (ACCESS-CM2, gold) against reanalyses. While MIROC6 captures the multi-decadal variability of the index (r = 0.79* vs. JRA-55), ACCESS-CM2 fails to replicate the observed temporal evolution (r = −0.19). These results demonstrate that the ability of ANNs to accurately predict WAM precipitation (as shown in Fig. 1) is fundamentally conditioned by the physical realism of the SLP teleconnections within the underlying CMIP6 training data.To isolate and robustly demonstrate the explicit added value of the physics-guided weighting strategy relative to a simpler alternative, we introduced a baseline benchmark consisting of the raw ensemble mean of the BEST Raws. This allows us to assess whether the physics-guided weighted projections might result simply from a subselection of models exhibiting accurate historical teleconnections or rather from the nonlinear operator capabilities inherent to the ANNs. As illustrated in Fig. 3, the “BEST ANNs” ensemble consistently outperforms the “BEST Raws” ensemble. Indeed, the shapes of the CDFs for the “Best ANNs” group (Fig. 3b) are closer to those of the observations (with the ensemble mean WD = 0.14) than those of the “Best Raws” group (Fig. 3a, with the ensemble WD = 0.84). Furthermore, the “Best ANNs” (Fig. 3c) predict a more realistic historical interannual variability of Sahel precipitation (r = 0.48) than the “Best Raws” models (r = −0.06). This improvement confirms that selecting historically skilled physics-based models is insufficient in itself, as the raw parameterizations of these models still inherit systematic biases regarding precipitation. Conversely, ANNs extract the physically coherent forced response from large-scale SLP predictors while filtering out structural deficiencies specific to GCMs.Fig. 3: Added value of the physics-guided weighting strategy over raw model selection in simulating WAM precipitation.Full size imageCumulative distribution functions (CDFs) for the Sahel June-September (JJAS) historical precipitation (1958–2014) from the BEST Raw CMIP6 models (a) and BEST ANNs-based reconstructions (b) relative to the CRU and GPCC observational datasets are shown. The Wasserstein Distance (WD) metric quantifies the mismatch between each model distribution and observations. The ANN ensemble (WD = 0.14) exhibits a substantially improved agreement with the observed precipitation distributions and reduces the WD relative to the raw-model ensemble (WD = 0.84). c Historical evolution of area-averaged JJAS Sahel precipitation from observations (OBS), the “BEST Raws” ensemble mean, and the weighted “BEST ANNs” ensemble mean. The ANNs-based ensemble mean more realistically reproduces the observed interannual-to-decadal variability (r = 0.48), while preserving physically consistent variability rather than collapsing toward an over-smoothed mean state. Correlation coefficients with observations are indicated in parentheses. d Temporal evolution of the historical inter-model spread (standard deviation) for the RAW and ANN ensembles (left y-axis) compared against the observational spread (right y-axis), defined as the standard deviation between CRU and GPCC. The ANN physics-guided weighting approach reduces the over-dispersiveness of the raw model range while successfully increasing the temporal co-variability with the observed spread (r = 0.37 for ANN vs. r = 0.07 for RAW models).Beyond improving mean climate states and variability, we evaluate whether our physics-guided reduction of the projected inter-model range might lead to an overconfident, under-dispersive spread envelope. To do so, we track the temporal evolution of the historical inter-model spread (standard deviation) and compare it against the observational spread derived from the discrepancy between CRU and GPCC (Fig. 3d). We found that the inter-model spread remains larger than the observational spread, which is physically consistent given that GCMs explore diverse climate sensitivities while observations rely on overlapping gauge networks. Specifically, while the RAW ensemble spread exhibits no temporal co-variability with observations (r = 0.07), the ANN-weighted spread shows a much stronger, positive correlation (r = 0.37) by capturing more similar interannual and decadal variability. This demonstrates that our physics-guided approach reduces the weights of dynamically inconsistent models while exploiting the ANN reconstructions to reveal a realistic envelope closer to observations.The pseudo-observation approach evaluates the ANNs’ internal dynamical consistencyWhile the analysis of teleconnections reveals physical consistency of the relationships learned by the ANNs, it does not totally guarantee their consistency when applied to future projections. A further evaluation step is therefore required before using the trained ANNs for climate change applications. To this end, we employ a pseudo-observation method, in which predicted precipitation from trained ANNs, forced by raw CMIP6 fields, is evaluated against the corresponding raw CMIP6 precipitation. This approach allows us to assess whether the ANNs preserve the internal physical coherence of each climate model, rather than introducing artificial relationships that are not present in the original simulations. Specifically, this ANNs’ check examines whether the precipitation predicted by the ANNs remains dynamically consistent with the internal physics simulated by the driving CMIP6 models, both under the historical and future climate. In this case, a close agreement between ANN-predicted and raw CMIP6 precipitation indicates that the ANNs act as physically informed emulators of the SLP boxes–precipitation relationship, rather than unconstrained statistical correctors. For most CMIP6 models, the correlation between ANN-predicted precipitation and raw model precipitation remains high in both historical and future periods, with values generally comparable to or exceeding the historical ANN-CRU benchmark value (r = 0.62; Fig. 4a). Additionally, the future vs. historical distributional shift is nearly identical for both the EnsMean of raw CMIP6 models and derived ANNs, as quantified by the values of WD = 0.43 for raw GCMs (Fig. 4b) and WD = 0.45 for ANNs (Fig. 4c). This means that while improving the distribution relative to observations (Fig. 1e), the ANNs remain physically anchored to the internal SMOPI SLP boxes-precipitation relationship of each driving raw CMIP6 model when forced by its own large-scale fields. As their physical consistency and statistical plausibility are established, we now utilize these trained ANNs to produce physics-guided weighted projections of future WAM precipitation. It is worth noting that this pseudo-observation experiment evaluates the internal dynamical consistency of the ANNs across realizations of the same GCM, rather than providing a direct observational validation of future projections. The observational constraint is subsequently introduced through the evaluation of the ANNs-derived relationships against JRA-55 and the application of the performance-based weighting scheme (see the “Methods” section).Fig. 4: Evaluation of ANN physical consistency and robustness using the pseudo-observation method.Full size imagea Correlation coefficients between ANN-predicted WAM precipitation and the corresponding raw CMIP6 models used for training. Performance is evaluated over the historical period (1958–2014, gold bars) and the future projection period (2015–2100, grey bars) under the SSP5-8.5 scenario. The horizontal dashed black line represents the correlation (r = 0.62) of the physics-weighted ANN EnsMean when forced by JRA-55 reanalysis against CRU observation. The high correlation values across both periods (generally r > 0.70) demonstrate that the ANNs successfully learn the underlying physical relationships between SMOPI SLP box predictors and precipitation within the model climate, maintaining this skill even under future greenhouse gas forcing. Comparison of cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) for June–September (JJAS) precipitation from raw CMIP6 (b) and their physics-weighted ANN counterparts (c). Black lines indicate the historical period, while red lines indicate the future period. Individual models are shown as thin lines, and the ensemble means (EnsMean) as thick solid lines. Observational benchmarks (CRU and GPCC) are indicated by dotted blue and gold lines, respectively. The shaded areas represent the inter-model spread for each period. The ANN model c more accurately reproduces historical distributions compared to observations than the raw CMIP6 data. b While consistently capturing the projected shift toward increased precipitation intensity in the future climate. These results validate the plausibility of the ANN approach for physics-guided weighted climate projections.ANNs’ physics-guided weighted projections reduce inter-model spreadsClimate models generally project diverse pathways of the WAM precipitation throughout the 21st century, in association with the diversity of physical representations of underlying processes7. Most of these physical processes are present in the SMOPI index18. We can reference here the contrasted patterns of change of CMIP6 models in the northern hemisphere differential sea surface temperature (SST) warming and inter-hemispheric temperature contrast, which induce inconsistent regional atmospheric circulation shifts, leading to various patterns of rainfall change over the Sahel3. The projected signals of the central Pacific ENSO22 and of tropical Atlantic Niño34, and therefore their teleconnections with WAM precipitation, are also other points of disagreement between the models. Reducing inter-model spreads in WAM precipitation projections, therefore, depends on forcing ANNs with teleconnections between the SMOPI SLP boxes and WAM precipitation as realistically as possible. However, projecting future WAM precipitation using ANNs trained only on historical data presents risks. ANNs trained only on historical data may suffer from non-stationarity and extrapolation issues when applied to future climate conditions35,36. To address this limitation, we retrained the ANNs using both historical and future periods (i.e., from 1958 to 2100) from member 1 (see subsection “ANNs: model architecture and training protocol” in the “Methods” section), thereby exposing them to the full range of projected climate states. The trained ANNs are then driven by SMOPI SLP box predictors from an independent ensemble member (member 2), ensuring physical consistency while reducing internal variability. This approach allows future dynamical changes to be directly propagated through the network and contributes to a reduction of projection diversity. In addition, as previously demonstrated, pseudo-observation experiments show that the ANN model preserves the magnitude and structure of the raw CMIP6 climate change signal, supporting the physical plausibility of the ANNs-based projections. We show projections separately from the two model groups (BEST ensemble and RESM ensemble) as well as from the full ensemble. This allows isolating the climate change signals that are grounded in physically realistic teleconnections from those influenced by less trustworthy large-scale relationships and quantifying their contribution to overall inter-model spread. The result of the full ensemble (ALL models) is also shown to provide a comprehensive view of the range of possible future projections and to facilitate comparison with conventional multi-model ensemble approaches. The ANNs-based projections significantly narrow the inter-model range compared to the raw CMIP6 ensemble (Fig. 5). They reduce the spread by 19.7% for BEST (Fig. 5a), 32.9% for RESM (Fig. 5b), and 30.0% for ALL models (Fig. 5c) by the end of the 21st century. Moreover, in the raw CMIP6 full ensemble, the RESM models dominate the inter-model spread budget, contributing approximately 69.1% of the total range, while the BEST models account for only 30.9% (Fig. 5a, b). This highlights that most of the spread in unconstrained projections originates from models with weaker performance in reproducing observed teleconnections. After applying the physics-guided weighted ANNs, the relative contribution of the BEST models increases to 34.8%, while that of the RESM models decreases to 65.2%. This redistribution of sources of inter-model spreads indicates that the ANNs effectively upweight physically consistent models and downweight less reliable ones without artificially collapsing the ensemble spread. Importantly, the full (ALL-model) ensemble (Fig. 5c) should be interpreted as a reference envelope rather than an independent contributor to spreads. The observed reduction in the total inter-model spread for ALL models, therefore, emerges from the internal rebalancing between BEST and RESM groups, rather than from a uniform shrinkage of model spread. Such a redistribution has important implications for flood risk, soil erosion, and water management in the WAM region39,40.DiscussionRefining models’ diversity in projections of WAM precipitation remains a major challenge for providing reliable climate services in the region. Despite CMIP6 models’ advances in complexity, they still show disparate results, alternating between significant drying and increased wetness3,4. Our results suggest that this spread is not limited to model resolution but is deeply linked to how models simulate large-scale atmospheric factors. By anchoring precipitation projections to the SMOPI SLP boxes, we move beyond simply comparing rainfall amounts to a process-oriented assessment of the physical mechanisms.The ability of ANNs to learn these relationships offers a considerable advantage over traditional ensemble means. While the ‘model democracy’ approach considers all simulations as equally plausible, our physics-guided weighted ANN recognizes that some models reproduce regional teleconnections much more realistically than others11. This is particularly evident when comparing the BEST and RESM model groups. We found that models with a more accurate representation of SMOPI dynamics tend to produce more constrained and physically consistent projections. Interestingly, a model can correlate well with observed precipitation for the wrong reasons, such as internal error compensation, if its underlying teleconnection schemes are unrealistic.In addition, the stability of the learned physical relationship between different members of the ensemble over time confirms the robustness of the deep learning architecture. By integrating historical and future climate states into the training process, ANNs can better account for potential non-stationarity in radiative forcing scenarios, such as the SSP5-8.5 scenario used in this study. Additionally, ANNs-based projections show clearer emerging signals of precipitation change, suggesting that conditioning on physically realistic circulation drivers isolates robust climate change responses from model noise. This helps bridge the gap between historical performance and future reliability, a common limitation of climate model weighting.A common concern when using ANNs trained with mean squared error (MSE) objectives under climate distributional shifts is the risk of “mode averaging” or artificial variance reduction, which can lead to ensemble responses featured by overconfidence and excessive smoothing. In the present study, however, the ANN optimization is driven by a Tweedie-based loss function combined with an amplitude-preserving constraint, rather than by a pure MSE objective alone. This hybrid formulation helps preserve the statistical distribution and intensity variability of precipitation fields while limiting excessive variance damping.However, when comparing the “BEST ANNs” and “BEST Raws”, it emerges that the ANN-based approach does not suffer from a collapse toward unrealistic mean solutions. Instead, the ANN ensemble preserves regional variability and physically interpretable spatial structures, which remain dynamically consistent with the behaviour of the underlying model. The reduction in inter-model spread, therefore, stems from the explicit synergy of our two-step approach rather than from statistical over-smoothing induced by the ANN optimization itself. First, the individual ANNs act as non-linear operators that filter out local model-specific parameterization biases, thereby reconstructing a physically cleaner and more coherent response within the ensemble. Second, the performance-based weighting scheme applies a complementary observational constraint by softly reducing the influence of dynamically inconsistent behaviours. Because our weighting approach uses a conservative, soft-constraint setup that avoids completely discarding models to prevent overconfidence (Supplementary Fig. 10), it does not act as an aggressive statistical filter. Instead, it works in conjunction with the ANN physical reconstructions to narrow the inter-model dispersion while fully preserving the forced response and internal variability inherent to each individual climate model.Although the present ANN architecture improves the dynamical coherence of precipitation projections across models, it does not fully eliminate structural climate-model uncertainty. Because the ANN learns relationships embedded within CMIP6 simulations, residual biases inherited from the driving models may still remain. Future work should therefore investigate more rigorous out-of-sample validation strategies, including perfect-model experiments and multi-model leave-one-out techniques and multi-member ANN training approaches to further isolate externally forced signals from the internal variability of specific realizations.The systematic shift toward higher rainfall intensities observed in our physics-guided weighted projections fits within the broader understanding of the intensification of the hydrological cycle in West Africa37,38. Even when mean rainfall changes remain moderate, the log-scale diagnostic of the distribution tails shows a shift toward higher thresholds, suggesting a robust increase in the frequency and intensity of heavy rainfall events under a warming climate. In a region where food security and water management are closely tied to monsoon variability, these observations, while constrained, provide a stronger scientific basis for adaptation strategies. This work also unveils that combining physical indices such as SMOPI and deep learning allows us to eliminate less reliable signals and reveal the future pathway where climate models achieve the highest physical consensus. This two-step paradigm can be easily transposed to other monsoonal systems or climate variables globally.MethodsModels and reanalysis datasetsDaily simulations of sea-level pressure (SLP) and precipitation from 11 CMIP6 models (see Supplementary Table 1), including the historical and Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP)-585 scenarios, are utilized in this work. On the one hand, using a daily time step ensures that the high-frequency variability footprint of some related monsoon processes, such as the African easterly waves, a major driver of the monsoon convective system41,42, is captured. On the other hand, it provides the ANN with a sufficiently large statistical sample for robust convergence, thus avoiding the smoothing of key physical processes when averaged monthly or yearly. By using the SSP585 scenario, we ensure that the climate change signal is sufficiently maximized to be distinguishable from natural variability. In doing so, we assess the ability of our method to constrain the most divergent future pathways and reduce the inter-model spread in a context of extreme radiative forcing.Models are selected so that each of them must be available on at least two realizations (member 1 and member 2), and the required variables, namely SLP and precipitation, must be available for each of the realizations. To ensure the robustness of results and avoid overfitting due to internal climate variability, we adopted a cross-validation strategy. For each of the 11 CMIP6 models, the CNN architecture was trained using member 1. Predictive performance and future projections (up to 2100) were then evaluated using an independent implementation, i.e., member 2. This procedure ensures that the deep learning model identifies stable physical teleconnections between sea-level pressure and precipitation, which are consistent for different initial conditions within the same CMIP6 model. Notably, although the two members have different internal variability, they share a common physics so that there are no physical inconsistencies when applying the model inter-member transfer learning17,33.ANN models are informed by climate models’ physics via teleconnections between the SLP boxes of the SMOPI system and the WAM precipitation. The observed teleconnections are extracted from the Japanese 55-year reanalysis (JRA-5519), which has a spatial resolution of 1.25° × 1.25°. Alongside JRA-55, we added the fifth-generation atmospheric reanalysis from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) (ERA543) to account for uncertainties in the reference datasets. Although ERA5 has a higher resolution than JRA-55, the latter is used as the reference dataset throughout the study. Indeed, relative to ERA5, JRA-55 better represents the interannual variability of WAM precipitation as well as its teleconnection with the SMOPI18. To ensure that generated predictions not only reflect the physics-based reanalyses but also are grounded in observed reality, two gridded observational products were included in analyses: the Climatic Research Unit gridded Time Series (CRU TS4.0844) observational dataset, with a resolution of 0.5° × 0.5°, and the Global Precipitation Climatology Center version 8 (GPCC) with a 0.5° × 0.5° grid spacing45. These two observational datasets were chosen not only for their reliability46 but also because of their availability from the beginning of the 20th century to the present day. As the production of the JRA-55 reanalysis only began in 1958, the historical data were selected from 1958 to 2014. The projections span from 2015 to 2100. All datasets were regridded to a common 1.25° × 1.25° resolution, matching the JRA-55 reference grid using the conservative remapping to minimize alterations in spatial gradients.Sahel monsoon ocean-pressure index (SMOPI)In this study, we aim to train ANN models to predict precipitation at a climatological scale. This requires transferring the physical processes that drive rainfall into ANNs. Precipitation in a region results from complex mechanisms that act at different scales, from local to global, and from hourly to multidecadal. Therefore, choosing the right predictor is essential for the ANNs to produce realistic results. The SMOPI is an ideal predictor for this task. Indeed, this index captures both large-scale, regional, and local features and thus global climate drivers of the Sahel monsoon system18. It is based on SLP in five specific regions of the tropical oceanic and continental basins. These regions were selected because their pressure variations are closely linearly and non-linearly linked to Sahel rainfall. The SMOPI is calculated as a weighted linear combination of the weighted box-averaged SLP values:$${{{SMOPI}}}=\frac{1}{4}({\beta }_{1}{{{{SLP}}}}_{1}+{\beta }_{2}{{{{SLP}}}}_{2}+{\beta }_{3}{{{{SLP}}}}_{3}+{\beta }_{4}{{{{SLP}}}}_{4})-{\beta }_{5}{{{{SLP}}}}_{5}$$
                    (1)
                where \({\beta }_{1},...,{\beta }_{5}\) are the weights for each SLP region, respectively, representing the size and shape of their grids and approximating their concrete contribution to the entire SMOPI strength. To apply the SMOPI formula, the SLP anomaly within each of the five SMOPI boxes (\({\beta }_{k}{{{{SLP}}}}_{k}\)) is calculated as a spatial area-weighted mean to account for the convergence of meridians toward the poles. Specifically, the weighted mean for a given box is defined as$${\beta }_{k}{{{{SLP}}}}_{k}\left(t\right)=\frac{{\varSigma }_{i,j}{{{SLP}}}\left(i,j,t\right){{{\rm{\cdot }}}} cos ({\phi }_{i})}{{\varSigma }_{i,j} cos ({\phi }_{i})}{{with}}\,k=({1},\,{2},\,{3},\,{4},\,{5})$$
                    (2)
                where \({{{SLP}}}\left(i,j,t\right)\) denotes the SLP at longitude grid point i, latitude grid point j, and at the time step t, and \({\phi }_{i}\) represents the latitude. This formulation ensures that the weighting factor depends exclusively on latitudinal geography and remains completely independent of the atmospheric variable being averaged.The intensity of SMOPI (\({I}_{{{\rm {SMOPI}}}}\)) is defined as the standardized anomaly of SMOPI, such that:$${I}_{SMOPI}=\frac{{{\rm {SMOPI}}}-\overline{{{\rm {SMOPI}}}}}{{\sigma }_{{{\rm {SMOPI}}}}}$$
                    (3)
                where \(\overline{SMOPI}\) is the long-term mean of SMOPI, and \({\sigma }_{{SMOPI}}\) represents its standard deviation. As defined, the SMOPI can be used across different scales, from subseasonal to multidecadal. Positive SMOPI intensity values correspond to stronger monsoon conditions, while negative values indicate weaker conditions. Although the SMOPI was originally developed for the Sahel region18, the large-scale pressure anomalies it captures are closely linked to the monsoon dynamics governing West Africa as a whole. Therefore, this study employs the SMOPI as a robust predictor for monsoon precipitation across the entire West African domain.ANNs: model architecture and training protocolANNs are used to learn the relationship between large-scale pressure patterns and WAM precipitation. In the same domain, CMIP6 models do not perform similarly compared to observations. Some are closer to observations than others, generally in association with the realism of their internal physics. However, the performance of a model also depends on its internal variability47. Even if a model has very realistic physics, it may not perfectly match observations due to its own chaotic fluctuations. This is why we trained each ANN on an individual model. This way, we avoid inconsistencies between the internal physical mechanisms of different models and ensure that each ANN learns the specific climate signals of its corresponding model. The ANN inputs consist of SLP fields extracted from the five SMOPI boxes (Supplementary Fig. 1), while the output corresponds to JJAS precipitation over West Africa on a regular latlon grid.The ANN is implemented as a convolutional neural network (CNN) with multiple parallel input branches (Conv-Branch 1–5; Fig. 6a). Each SMOPI SLP box is processed independently through a dedicated convolutional branch composed of two convolutional layers followed by adaptive average pooling. This design helps the network to extract spatial features specific to each pressure region. The outputs of all branches are subsequently concatenated and passed through a series of completely connected dense layers, which learn the combined influence of the different SLP regions. The final layer reshapes the output into a two-dimensional latlon precipitation field. The Tweedie component48 is ideal for precipitation because it effectively models data with many zeros and a continuous positive distribution. We improved the model’s ability to capture extreme events by adding an amplitude constraint. This constraint uses a normalized mean squared error (MSE) to ensure the model properly simulates the intensity and phase of the monsoon49. For all rounds of the training process, we used the TensorFlow package, applied a learning rate of 10−3, and a dropout regularization of 0.2 in all convolutional branches to reduce overfitting. The batch size corresponds to the full training set, as the predictors and targets are provided as complete temporal samples. Each convolutional layer uses 32 filters, and the same architecture was used across all realizations, each realization running over 500 epochs. This is because precipitation is a non-negative, highly skewed variable characterized by a mixture of zero and positive values. It can therefore be approximated by a Poisson–Gamma (Tweedie) distribution, which accounts for both dry events and continuous rainfall intensities. Models whose ANN-derived teleconnection structures more closely reproduce the JRA-55 dynamical relationships predict more realistic precipitation and receive larger weights in the final ensemble.ANNs’ ensemble-mean construction approachClimate model projections are commonly analysed using a simple ensemble mean, where all models are weighted equally7. This ‘model democracy’ approach reduces random errors, but it assumes that all models are equally realistic. While other studies use weighted ensembles, they often calculate weights using raw data10,52. This preserves internal model noise, which can lead to spurious results. In this study, we use ANNs to create a physics-weighted multi-ANN ensemble mean. Here, weights reflect how closely each CMIP6-driven ANN matches the JRA-55 reanalysis, which we use as the reference for realistic atmospheric dynamics. The weight assigned to the i-th ANN is defined as the likelihood that observations originate from that ANN. In practice, the likelihood of the ith CMIP6-driven ANN is expressed as a generalized distance-based Softmax function53 controlled by a temperature (or sharpness) scaling parameter τ defined as$${w}_{i}=\frac{exp (-\frac{{d}_{i}^{2}}{2\tau })}{{\sum }_{j=1}^{N}exp (-\frac{{d}_{j}^{2}}{2\tau })}$$
                    (6)
                where di is the normalized distance between the CMIP6-driven ANN output and the observation, expressed as$${d}_{i}=\sqrt{2\left(1-{r}_{i}\right)}$$
                    (7)
                where \({r}_{i}\) is the spatially averaged Fisher z-transformed and back-transformed temporal correlation of grid points between the ith CMIP6-driven ANN output and the observation. Under the default conservative setup (τ = 1), substituting the distance metric (Eq. 7) into the Softmax likelihood formulation (Eq. (6)) algebraically simplifies to a function directly scaling with the correlation coefficient:$${w}_{i}=\frac{exp ({r}_{i}-1)}{{\sum }_{j=1}^{N}exp ({r}_{j}-1)}$$
                    (8)
                where N is the total number of ANNs in the ensemble. This analysis demonstrates that the default setup used (Eq. (8)) acts as a safe, conservative, soft constraint that retains ensemble diversity. We deliberately focus on this soft-constraint approach because it avoids overconfidence by accounting for the shared signal of the majority of the models, rather than aggressively favouring a single outlier. This approach fosters the combined effects of the weighting scheme and the physics-guided ANN reconstruction, both of which contribute to the overall reduction in inter-model spread. Quantifying UK coastal flood exposure under future sea-level rise to 2300
                    M. D. Palmer 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-7422-198X1,2, J. Savage 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-4807-09163, P. D. Bates

Subjects
        
            Climate-change impactsProjection and prediction

AbstractThe latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessment report highlighted the potential for more than 15 m of global sea-level rise by 2300. In this study, we explore the implications for UK coastal flood exposure by combining national-scale flood modelling with physically-based storylines of UK sea-level rise. By 2100 all storylines show broadly similar results with at least an additional 0.5 million people exposed to the 1-in-200 year undefended flood extent, which represents a 25% increase compared to present day. Under the most pessimistic storyline by 2300 involving significant ice-sheet instability, an additional 13 million people could be exposed to the 1-in-200 year undefended flood event. This would imply the potential need for large-scale movement of populations and settlements away from the coast in the coming centuries. Given current global emissions pledges, exposure increases by 1.7 million people by 2300, however up to 1 million could be avoided if Paris Agreement targets for greenhouse gas emissions are met.

                        IntroductionSea-level rise poses an existential threat to coastal communities and ecosystems around the world1. Global mean sea level (GMSL) increased by about 20 ± 5 cm over the period 1901–2018, with a marked acceleration since the 1960s2. Since the 1990s, the net contribution from ice sheet mass loss has increased by a factor of four, and these huge ice reservoirs remain the primary threat for sea-level rise in the coming centuries2,3. The UK is an ideal natural laboratory in which to examine the implications of these possible changes, given the large coastal flood exposure and complex interaction of different sea-level rise drivers for this location. While the observed increase in UK-average sea level of 18 ± 3 cm over the period 1900–2022 is in good agreement with GMSL, there are important spatial variations in the UK rate of rise associated with Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA)4. In England alone, a recent study suggests that there are currently 544,000 residential and 72,000 non-residential properties in the coastal floodplain, an amount equivalent to 2.5% of the total national building stock5. Even when flood defences are accounted for, approximately 10% of these coastal floodplain properties are exposed to events with a return period of less than 75 years. This could increase substantially under sea-level rise scenarios, and this has the potential to significantly reshape the geography of the UK coast.Previous studies have highlighted the consequences of climate policy decisions in the next few decades for determining sea-level rise outcomes for centuries and millennia to come, illustrating the importance of early emissions reductions and raising questions about intergenerational justice2,6,7. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report of Working Group I (IPCC AR6) stated that by 2300, GMSL will increase by 0.3–3.1 m under low emissions (SSP1-2.6) and 1.7–6.8 m under high emissions (SSP5-8.5), increasing up to 16 m for SSP5-8.5 if uncertain ice sheet instability processes are included2,8. This wide range of potential outcomes has motivated recent studies to pursue a storyline approach, where a small number of singular and physically-consistent trajectories of future sea-level rise are generated that span the overall uncertainty space9,10.The current national UK sea-level projections do not include the possibility of accelerated sea-level rise associated with uncertain ice sheet instability processes11,12, and current UK guidance on a “credible maximum (H++)” sea-level rise by 2100 is 1.9 m13 (www.gov.uk/guidance/flood-and-coastal-risk-projects-schemes-and-strategies-climate-change-allowances), yet sea-level rise in London could reach 5 m by 2150 and more than 15 m by 2300, based on outcomes highlighted in IPCC AR62,8,10. Therefore, the goal of the present study is to provide a comprehensive analysis of the implications of IPCC AR6 sea-level projections out to 2300 for UK coastal flooding and coastline retreat. While coastal flood hazard is also subject to changes in storm surges, waves and tides, these are secondary factors compared to the century timescale threat from sea-level rise14 and therefore neglected from this study.Current estimates of coastal flooding produced by the UK Government and others often use so-called ‘bathtub models’ to predict inundation. These take the extreme water level at the coast and project it inland, with the assumption that any land below this elevation is inundated even if, in practice, this is physically impossible due to dynamical effects or a lack of hydraulic connectivity15. Recent high-profile global studies looking at sea-level rise impacts16,17,18,19,20 also invariably use bathtub methods. Instead, to realistically model coastal inundation, a numerical hydrodynamic model is needed that properly represents the physics and time dynamics of shallow water flow. Such models have previously only existed for individual coastal segments or river reaches, but recently the availability of better data, new numerical schemes and High Performance Computing has allowed hydrodynamic approaches to be applied to simulate flooding at national to global scales21,22,23,24.Our analysis is based on model simulations without flood defences for several reasons. Firstly, it allows us to identify: (i) new populations that could become exposed to flooding in the absence or failure of flood defences; (ii) infrastructure or land that could become exposed to floods, which could help inform decisions on whether areas require future investment in flood protection infrastructure; and (iii) locations that could be repurposed for relocated communities to inhabit. Secondly, there are no datasets that project flood defence standards out to 2300, and the level of investment in defences would also likely vary depending on the climate scenario followed. Lastly, if we assume defences remain at their current standards of protection, we would learn very little about changing flood risk except in undefended and rural areas. Therefore, we feel that the undefended scenario provides a more complete picture of potential exposure to floods both in the present day and the future. We work with the present day population as a baseline because currently available UK future projections25 are: (i) ‘blind’ to flood risk and therefore allow expansion of population into areas which, in reality, would never be developed; (ii) only available at 1 km resolution which is insufficiently granular for a localised problem such as flooding; and (iii) only exist out to 2100 as beyond this uncertainties are simply too great. It should be noted, however, that the population is not static and future work should incorporate these effects once appropriate projections become available.This study uses a recently published set of physically-consistent storylines of UK future sea-level rise that span the full range of potential outcomes to 2300 across the low emissions (SSP1-2.6) and high emissions (SSP5-8.5) scenarios, including ice sheet collapse, highlighted in IPCC AR63,10. While we acknowledge that high emissions futures are considered unlikely26, the sea-level rise outcomes associated with simulations run under these scenarios are important for a more complete understanding of the total risk landscape and for risk-averse decision contexts27,28. These are then used within the 1 arcsecond (25 m) spatial resolution whole UK hydrodynamic model of Bates et al.23 to simulate the area at risk of flooding during storm events, given the different sea-level rise scenarios. This whole UK model is unique in being able to simulate coastal inundation from any plausible boundary conditions with fine spatial resolution and high skill (see “Methods” for more details). The storylines are based on the same underlying projection machinery as the UKCP18 sea-level projections11,29 and are therefore consistent with that information, which forms the basis of current UK planning. The results presented here are based on the five storylines of future UK sea-level rise from Palmer et al.10 with a focus on two for the flood modelling results. Storyline B is used as a baseline scenario and is broadly consistent with current international greenhouse gas emissions pledges. Storyline H2 is used as a “reasonable worst case scenario” under high greenhouse gas emissions and includes representation of poorly-understood ice sheet instability processes (see Supplementary Note S1). While both H1 and H2 could be used as a reasonable worst-case scenario, we focus on H2 because it corresponds to the Low-Likelihood High-Impact storyline that was given prominence in the IPCC AR6 Summary for Policymakers and more completely illustrates the risk that could be avoided through effective global action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions28. In this work, we characterise the coastal flood impacts at 2100, 2200 and 2300 associated with the sea-level rise storylines given the present-day population for the UK as a whole and for the UK capital cities of Belfast, Cardiff, London and Edinburgh. Simulations are based on the 1-in-200-year return period extreme coastal water level event from the UK Environment Agency coastal flood boundary condition dataset (see “Methods”) since this is the typical design standard of UK coastal flood defences in urban areas.ResultsSea-level rise storylines and spatial patternsThe storylines used in this study represent a broad range of outcomes for global mean sea-level (GMSL) rise from less than 1 m to more than 16 m by 2300 (Fig. 1a, Table 1). Story A, B and C show a near-linear rise of GMSL and span the overall range of the likely projections from IPCC AR6 across the SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 emissions scenarios. Storylines H1 and H2 show a marked acceleration in GMSL rise between 2050 and 2150 associated with ice sheet instabilities and correspondingly much larger rates and magnitudes of sea-level rise over the coming centuries. The model simulations underlying the storylines are based on assumptions of reducing greenhouse gas emissions30 from the 2020 s (Storyline A), around 2040 (Storyline B) or from 2150 (Storylines C, H1, H2) with a subsequent decrease in the rate of GMSL rise thereafter (Fig. 1a). The local expression of relative sea-level rise across the UK and Ireland in the coming centuries shows large spatial variations from the global average that results from three main factors: (i) the ongoing effects on local sea level from GIA31; and the spatial patterns of change associated with the (ii) Greenland and (iii) Antarctic ice sheets10,32. Spatial patterns of sea-level rise at 2300 for Storylines A and B (Fig. 1b, c) are dominated by GIA with the characteristic pattern of vertical land uplift in the north and land subsidence in the south. For example, this effect substantially reduces the 2300 sea-level rise values for Belfast and Edinburgh to about 0.1–0.2 m, compared to 0.6–0.7 m for Cardiff and London in Storyline A. Storyline C also exhibits a strong imprint of GIA in the spatial pattern of sea-level rise (Fig. 1d) with values across the UK ranging from 3.5–4.5 m. The influence of spatial patterns associated with the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets is more evident for Storylines H1 and H2 (Fig. 1e, f), with values at 2300 ranging from about 8.5–9.5 m and 16.5–17.5 m, respectively.Fig. 1: sea-level rise storylines and 2300 spatial patterns.Full size imagea Time series of global mean sea-level (GMSL) rise for the five storylines presented in Palmer et al.10 as indicated in the figure legend. The grey-shaded region shows the overall IPCC AR6 likely range (i.e., the central two-thirds probability distribution) across the SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 greenhouse gas emissions scenarios to 2150. The grey dotted line shows the IPCC AR6 low-likelihood high-impact storyline presented in the Working Group I Summary for Policymakers3. b–f The spatial pattern of relative sea-level rise at 2300 associated with each storyline. All sea-level rise projections are expressed relative to the 1986–2005 average.Table 1 Summary of sea-level rise storylines used in this studyFull size tableThe flood mapping and impacts analysis presented here focuses on Storyline B as a baseline scenario (in the absence of further global greenhouse gas emissions pledges) and Storyline H2 as a “reasonable worst case” scenario for informing future coastal adaptation planning. We choose Storyline B as our baseline rather than Storyline A because the latter could be considered an overly optimistic basis for adaptation planning, given that it goes beyond current emissions pledges and assumes a weak sea-level response to future warming (Table 1). While we cannot give a robust likelihood for Storyline H2, we assess that it is broadly consistent with the UK National Risk Register definition of “reasonable worst case” of being “a challenging manifestation of the scenario after highly implausible scenarios are excluded” and note that IPCC AR6 states that this outcome cannot be ruled out under high emissions3. For a discussion of what constitutes “reasonable” in this context, please see Supplementary Note S1. GMSL rise at 2100 reaches approximately 0.6 m for Storyline B and 1.5 m for Storyline H2 (Fig. 1a), with large geographical variations across the UK and Ireland (Supplementary Fig. 1).Impacts of sea-level rise on UK coastal flood hazardAt a national scale, the changes in undefended inundation from a 1-in-200 year storm surge event (i.e., the basis of flood defence standards in the UK) shows modest changes with future sea-level rise at 2100 (Fig. 2A). The greatest areas of increased inundation are found for The Wash and the Humber Estuary on the east coast of England with a 13% national increase in total flood extent for Storyline B and 41% increase for Storyline H2 (Fig. 2A, Supplementary Table 3). To illustrate the local impacts of sea-level rise, we also present detailed mapping for the UK capital cities of Belfast (2B), Cardiff (2C), Edinburgh (2D) and London (2E), along with the present-day area at risk. For Storyline B by 2100, the additional areas of inundation are relatively modest. Given climate change and uncertainty tolerances within flood defence design33, it is likely that the real-world impacts of a ~ 0.5 m sea-level rise in areas protected by coastal flood defences would be limited. Nevertheless, many UK port facilities in southern England, which are necessarily outside of flood defences, will be impacted by a ~ 0.5 m rise in sea level due to the increase in extreme water levels during coastal surge events, and this may require additional protection measures to be adopted following port planning guidance and sector-specific climate change risk assessments34,35. For scenario H2 by 2100, the UK sea-level rise range of 1.2–1.5 m is more problematic, with large areas of west London, central Cardiff and infrastructure such as Belfast Airport within the zone inundated by the 1-in-200 year event. For H2, sea-level rise by 2100 is at the upper limit of what any present-day defences could plausibly protect against, so we can more definitively say these are areas that are not currently at risk but would be in the future.Fig. 2: Flood maps including sea-level rise to 2100.Full size imageA Flood inundation map for the UK based on the 1-in-200-year return period for the present day and with sea-level rise for Storylines B and H2 at 2100 in the absence of flood defences, as indicated in the figure legend. Panels B–E show local flood maps for Belfast, Cardiff, Edinburgh and London.By 2300, both Storyline B and Storyline H2 imply dramatic changes for the UK coastal flood hazard (Fig. 3A). The Storyline B local relative sea-level rise of about 1.2–1.8 m across the UK translates, in the absence of flood defences, to a 56% increase in the flood area of the 1-in-200-year storm surge event (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Table 3). For Storyline H2, the local sea-level rise at 2300 ranges from about 16.5–17.5 m with more than a 300% increase in flood area for the 1-in-200-year surge event (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Table 3). For this amount of sea-level rise, present-day flood defences are largely irrelevant. At a national scale, for H2, it is The Wash and the Humber Estuary that show the largest change in area of land exposed to coastal flood hazard. However, we can now also see evidence of substantive changes in other parts of the United Kingdom, including the Thames estuary, Eastern Norfolk, North Somerset, Gloucestershire, Liverpool and the northwest coast of England. As before, Fig. 3 shows the details of inundation changes for the UK capital cities. Under Storyline B by 2300, some major public institutions, such as the Welsh parliament building (the Senedd) in Cardiff, now lie within the 200-year flood zone, along with major UK infrastructure such as Glasgow airport, Teesside chemical works and the port of Dover. In Storyline H2, many UK critical infrastructure locations are affected by flooding, including the M25 motorway (especially around Heathrow airport) and the financial district of the City of London. Nationally significant heritage, such as St. Paul’s Cathedral in London, lies within the flood zone, and large areas of west and north London are impacted by water depths in excess of 1 m. Along the east coast, the upland area of the Lincolnshire Wolds becomes an island during extreme floods, and coastal flooding here can even propagate inland as far as major cities such as Cambridge and York, both of which see their entire central areas flooded to depths of 1 m or more. Panels B–E show local flood maps for Belfast, Cardiff, Edinburgh and London.The inundation maps have been combined with present-day UK population data36 to estimate the potential change in the population exposed to the 1-in-200 year flood event for each of the five storylines at 2100, 2200 and 2300 (Fig. 4). At 2100, all five storylines yield a modest increase in population exposure relative to the present day, with results indicating a low sensitivity to emissions pathways on this time-horizon. This outcome relates to the committed sea-level rise inherent to all storylines that is associated with past greenhouse gas emissions and the slow response of the ocean and cryosphere to surface warming2 (Supplementary Fig. 1). By 2200 there are much greater differences across the storylines associated with the broader range of sea-level rise outcomes (Supplementary Fig. 2) and even reductions in population exposure in Northern Ireland and Scotland for Storylines A and B where ongoing vertical land uplift associated with GIA overcomes the climate-change-induced sea-level rise.
